case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FIFRA preempts a Missouri state-law failure-to-warn claim seeking a cancer warning for an EPA-registered pesticide label when EPA has concluded such a warning is not required and any label change would require EPA approval.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 7 U.S.C. §§ 136 et seq., especially the express preemption provision in 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b) (state "requirements for labeling or packaging" different from or in addition to FIFRA) and FIFRA’s EPA label-approval/registration scheme (including the prohibition on selling a pesticide with labeling that differs from the EPA-approved label).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Monsanto argues that respondent’s failure-to-warn theory would impose a state-law "labeling requirement" that is "in addition to" or "different from" the EPA-approved labeling decisions under FIFRA, and therefore is expressly preempted by § 136v(b). The core point is that EPA has already considered the relevant risk information and determined that the specific warning demanded by the state tort claim is not required; because Monsanto cannot unilaterally add that warning without EPA approval, a damages verdict effectively forces a label change and conflicts with FIFRA’s uniform, federal labeling regime. Monsanto also emphasizes a broader need for national uniformity in pesticide labeling and contends that allowing juries to mandate extra warnings via tort verdicts recreates the very patchwork Congress barred—especially where EPA has affirmatively rejected the warning at issue.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Durnell argues that FIFRA does not categorically preempt traditional state tort failure-to-warn claims and that his claim enforces, rather than adds to, federal standards because FIFRA requires labels not be "misbranded" and to contain adequate warnings. In that framing, state tort law provides a parallel remedy when a label is allegedly inadequate. He also contends that EPA registration/approval is not a definitive federal determination that a warning is unnecessary for all purposes, and that manufacturers retain avenues to seek EPA approval for strengthened warnings; thus, compliance with both state tort duties and FIFRA is not impossible. Respondent further argues that recognizing preemption here would improperly convert EPA’s regulatory judgments into broad tort immunity absent clear congressional direction.
key_precedents: Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, 544 U.S. 431 (2005)
Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett, 570 U.S. 472 (2013)
Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht, 587 U.S. 299 (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh rightly emphasize that § 136v(b) expressly preempts state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and that a damages verdict can function as a compulsory labeling mandate. But under Bates, the essential narrowing inquiry is whether the state duty is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s own misbranding/adequate-warning standard or instead imposes a distinct label-content command, and that cannot be resolved merely by pointing to EPA registration or an agency view that a cancer warning is “not required.” Absent an authoritative, force-of-law EPA disallowance of the specific warning at issue—as Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht caution when treating agency action as foreclosing stronger warnings—I do not see a sufficient basis to conclude the Missouri verdict necessarily demanded “different” labeling rather than enforcing FIFRA’s health-protective warning obligation. Justice Thomas’s textual point that a verdict is a “requirement” does not, on this record, answer whether it is “in addition to” federal law; reading registration as a prohibition would collapse Bates’s parallel-claims pathway and expand preemption beyond the narrowest ground supported here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest contention is that, under Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht, preemption should require “clear evidence” that EPA would have rejected the precise cancer warning, lest registration become tort immunity. But that framework addresses implied conflict preemption; here Congress enacted an express command in § 136v(b) barring any state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and (as Bates itself recognized) common-law verdicts can be “requirements” in the ordinary textual sense. Even if FIFRA’s misbranding standard is general, a Missouri jury rule compelling additional label text beyond EPA-approved labeling is “different” from the federal requirement as implemented, and the absence of a separate, formal EPA “rejection order” does not negate the statute’s preemptive text. Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s point reinforces the practical and legal structure: because FIFRA makes lawful labeling contingent on EPA approval, the state duty operates as an add-on labeling mandate that Congress prohibited, regardless of whether Monsanto might later petition the agency.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the best objection: under Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht we should demand “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected the precise cancer warning, lest registration become de facto tort immunity. But that framework fits implied conflict preemption; here Congress wrote an express rule in § 136v(b), and the Missouri verdict functions as a state-law “requirement for labeling” that is “in addition to or different from” the EPA-approved label—so the key question is parallelism under Bates, not Albrecht’s evidentiary threshold. Where EPA has made a product-specific determination that a cancer warning is not required, a state duty to add that warning is not “equivalent” to FIFRA’s misbranding standard as implemented; it supplants the uniform labeling judgment Congress assigned to EPA. Justice Thomas’s point reinforces mine: Monsanto’s ability to petition EPA does not cure that the state verdict compels different label content despite FIFRA’s bar on unilateral deviations, bringing this squarely within § 136v(b).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that a damages verdict effectively compels new label content and Monsanto lacks unilateral authority to change it—has force, but it still assumes the state duty is necessarily “in addition to” federal law rather than parallel to FIFRA’s own misbranding/adequate-warning requirement under Bates. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the decisive question for me is whether EPA, acting with force-of-law effect, actually disallowed the specific cancer warning; absent that kind of authoritative federal rejection, treating registration plus a “not required” view as a binding no-warning command would collapse Bates’s parallel-claims space into near-total tort immunity. Justice Thomas is right that § 136v(b) is express preemption and that verdicts can be “requirements,” but express preemption still demands a meaningful comparator: if the state rule simply enforces FIFRA’s health-protective warning standard, it is not “different from” federal law unless EPA has made clear that this particular warning cannot appear. Given this record, Petitioners have not carried the burden to show the Missouri verdict imposed a genuinely additional labeling requirement rather than a parallel one that protects injured plaintiffs when federal oversight proves incomplete.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is textual and structural: a verdict can be a state “requirement for labeling,” and FIFRA does not allow Monsanto to unilaterally change the label, so the Missouri duty can look like an extra state mandate. But Bates makes the decisive comparison to FIFRA’s own misbranding/adequate-warning standard, not to whatever label EPA happened to approve at registration; without an authoritative, force-of-law EPA decision rejecting this specific cancer warning, I don’t see how the state duty is necessarily “in addition to or different from” federal requirements rather than parallel to them. Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch treat EPA’s view that a warning is “not required” as a binding federal prohibition, yet § 136v(b) preempts only state requirements different from federal ones, and “not required” is not the same as “forbidden” absent clear regulatory action. Chief Justice Roberts’s Wyeth/Merck framing therefore remains persuasive as a pragmatic way to operationalize Bates’s parallel-claim boundary and avoid reading registration as across-the-board tort immunity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief and Justice Kagan press the strongest counter: that Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht require “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected this precise cancer warning, and that Bates preserves parallel state duties. But that framing fits conflict/impossibility preemption; here Congress enacted an express rule in § 136v(b), so the textual question is whether the Missouri verdict imposes a state “requirement for labeling” “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s. As Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize, a damages verdict that compels adding a cancer warning beyond the EPA-approved label functions as an additional labeling mandate, and FIFRA’s structure—requiring EPA approval before label changes—means the state duty does not merely run “parallel” to federal law as administered. Wyeth/Albrecht cannot be used to rewrite § 136v(b) into a clear-evidence prerequisite for express preemption, and accepting Respondent’s approach would let juries negate the uniform labeling regime Congress chose.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Wyeth/Merck v. Albrecht “clear evidence” point is the strongest response, but I continue to think it belongs to conflict/impossibility preemption and cannot be imported to narrow FIFRA’s express preemption text in § 136v(b). Under Bates (as Justice Thomas emphasizes), a common-law verdict can be a state “requirement for labeling,” and here the Missouri duty—operating through damages pressure—effectively mandates adding a cancer warning different from the EPA-approved label, so it is “in addition to or different from” the federal scheme. Justice Kagan’s concern about collapsing Bates’s parallel-claims pathway is serious, but in my view the claim is not genuinely “parallel” once it requires specific warning content that EPA has not required and that Monsanto cannot implement unilaterally (as Justice Alito’s Mensing/Bartlett analogy underscores). Institutional and practical considerations cut the same way: allowing 50-state juries to impose divergent label content defeats the national uniformity Congress assigned to EPA through registration and § 136v(b).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Wyeth/Merck “clear evidence” framework is the strongest argument for Respondent, but it is aimed at conflict/impossibility preemption and cannot supplant the express-preemption text Congress enacted in § 136v(b). Under that text, as Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, a common-law verdict that effectively compels adding a cancer warning is a state “requirement for labeling” that is “in addition to or different from” the EPA-approved labeling scheme, and Bates preserves only genuinely parallel duties—not ones that mandate different label content. Even accepting Justice Kagan’s concern about tort immunity, the relevant comparator is the federal “requirement” as implemented through EPA’s product-specific label approval; a jury-imposed warning requirement that goes beyond that is not merely enforcing FIFRA’s misbranding floor but altering the federally operative label. Justice Alito’s Mensing/Bartlett point reinforces that, because if the manufacturer cannot lawfully implement the warning unilaterally, the state duty functions as an extra labeling mandate of the sort § 136v(b) forbids.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Mensing/Bartlett analogy remains the Petitioners’ most serious point because it highlights Monsanto’s inability to change labels unilaterally, but those cases turned on a federal scheme that itself made the stronger warning unlawful absent a specific pathway; here, I do not see comparable, product-specific EPA action with force-of-law that actually disallowed the precise cancer warning a jury might find necessary to avoid FIFRA misbranding. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Bates preserves failure-to-warn claims that run parallel to FIFRA’s own “adequate warnings” requirement, and reading § 136v(b) to preempt whenever EPA has registered a label would convert registration into tort immunity and collapse Bates’s parallel-claims pathway. Justice Thomas’s textual point that a verdict is a “requirement” does not resolve whether it is “in addition to” federal law, because the proper comparator is FIFRA’s misbranding standard—not EPA’s discretionary decision not to demand more on this record. Under Merck v. Albrecht’s focus on an authoritative agency disallowance, generalized EPA views and registration do not establish that the state duty conflicts rather than parallels federal law, so I am not persuaded to switch.

John Roberts.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and Bates v. Dow Agrosciences holds that common-law failure-to-warn claims survive where they impose “parallel requirements” to FIFRA’s misbranding and adequate-warning standards. EPA registration and approval, standing alone, is not a clear congressional command to displace traditional state tort remedies, and under our conflict-preemption cases a defendant must show true impossibility—i.e., that it could not comply with both federal law and state duty—rather than a generalized assertion of federal regulatory primacy. Consistent with Wyeth v. Levine and Merck Sharp & Dohme v. Albrecht, the question is whether there is clear evidence EPA would have rejected the specific warning demanded; absent such a showing on this record, we should resolve the case on narrow grounds by allowing the state claim to proceed without converting EPA’s registration decision into broad tort immunity.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause provides that a State "shall not impose or continue in effect any requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from" those required under the Act. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). A Missouri failure-to-warn verdict demanding a cancer warning would operate as a state-law “requirement for labeling,” because it effectively compels Monsanto to alter the EPA-approved label to avoid liability, yet FIFRA’s scheme forbids distributing a pesticide with labeling that differs from the EPA-approved labeling and requires EPA approval for such changes. Although Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC recognized a narrow space for state duties that are “equivalent to, and fully consistent with” FIFRA’s misbranding provisions, 544 U.S. 431, 447 (2005), a claim seeking a warning the EPA has affirmatively concluded is not required is not “equivalent” but “in addition to” the federal determination, and thus is expressly preempted under the statute’s text and uniformity purpose.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FIFRA expressly preempts any state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC that category includes common-law failure-to-warn duties when they function as labeling mandates. Here, the Missouri verdict effectively imposes a cancer-warning requirement that is not “in fact” genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s federal labeling determination, particularly where EPA has affirmatively concluded that such a warning is not required and Monsanto cannot add it unilaterally without EPA approval. As in PLIVA, Inc. v. Mensing and Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett, it is no answer that the manufacturer could ask the agency to change the label; the operative question is whether federal law permits the manufacturer independently to comply with the state-imposed duty. Allowing juries to impose additional warnings despite EPA’s contrary labeling decision would undermine FIFRA’s uniform national labeling scheme and produce the patchwork Congress sought to prevent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars only state "requirements for labeling or packaging" that are "in addition to or different from" federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC a state failure-to-warn verdict is not preempted to the extent it enforces a duty genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard requiring adequate warnings (i.e., a parallel requirement). EPA registration and its view that a cancer warning is not required do not, without a clear and authoritative determination that the agency would forbid the warning, convert that regulatory judgment into tort immunity—particularly where the manufacturer retains a pathway to seek EPA approval for stronger warnings, consistent with Wyeth v. Levine’s insistence on a demanding showing for conflict preemption. On this record, Monsanto has not shown the kind of “impossibility” or definitive federal prohibition necessary under the conflict-preemption framework reflected in Wyeth and Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht, so Missouri’s traditional failure-to-warn remedy may proceed as a backstop protecting injured persons.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 136v(b) expressly preempts only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” FIFRA, but Bates v. Dow Agrosciences holds that common-law failure-to-warn duties survive when they are “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standard—i.e., they enforce the federal requirement that labeling not be misleading and include necessary warnings. EPA registration and a conclusion that a particular warning is not “required” do not, without a clear and binding federal disallowance, automatically convert a state tort duty into an “additional” labeling requirement; the core question is whether the state rule demands content that conflicts with FIFRA’s own adequacy standard. Consistent with Wyeth v. Levine and Merck v. Albrecht, the manufacturer must show that federal law made compliance with both regimes impossible (or that EPA would have rejected the specific warning with force-of-law effect), and the mere need to seek EPA approval for a label change does not itself establish such a conflict. Reading § 136v(b) to categorically bar damages actions whenever EPA has registered the label would collapse Bates’s parallel-requirements pathway and create broad tort immunity without clear congressional instruction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: FIFRA’s text expressly bars any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences, common-law duties (including failure-to-warn) can constitute “requirements,” and they escape preemption only if they are genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standards; here, however, the Missouri claim seeks a specific cancer warning that EPA has affirmatively deemed not required, so a damages verdict would function as a state-imposed additional labeling requirement. Because FIFRA forbids selling a pesticide with labeling that differs from the EPA-approved label absent EPA approval, the state-law duty as applied would compel a label change that federal law does not demand and thus is “in addition to,” triggering § 136v(b) and the separation-of-powers concern of allowing juries to override the federal labeling judgment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: FIFRA expressly preempts state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law failure-to-warn duties can qualify as “requirements,” and a state rule demanding a particular warning that differs from what EPA requires for that pesticide is preempted; here, EPA has concluded the cancer warning is not required, so a Missouri damages verdict effectively imposes a different label requirement. Given FIFRA’s regime that prohibits distribution with labeling that departs from the EPA-approved label absent EPA approval, the state-law claim functions as a de facto command to change the label and undermines the uniformity Congress sought, making the claim preempted under § 136v(b) as construed in Bates.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: FIFRA expressly bars States from imposing “any requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” those required under FIFRA, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and Bates confirms that common-law duties (including failure-to-warn) can qualify as “requirements” if they would compel a label change rather than merely mirror federal standards. Here, EPA has affirmatively concluded that the cancer warning sought is not required on the registered label, and the manufacturer cannot unilaterally add it without EPA approval; a state-law damages verdict would therefore functionally impose an additional labeling requirement that diverges from the federally approved labeling determination. Under the methodological approach reflected in Mensing and Bartlett, when federal law withholds unilateral authority to change the label and the state duty would require that change, the state claim is preempted. Because the demanded warning is not “parallel” to the federal labeling requirement as applied by EPA to this product, the claim falls within § 136v(b)’s express preemption.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), bars state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, but Bates v. Dow Agrosciences held that common-law duties can survive when they impose “parallel requirements” that track FIFRA’s misbranding standard rather than add new labeling obligations. A Missouri failure-to-warn verdict here can be understood as enforcing the federal duty not to market a “misbranded” pesticide—i.e., one lacking warnings “necessary … to protect health,” 7 U.S.C. § 136(q)(1)(G)—unless EPA has made a clear, case-specific determination that adding the precise cancer warning would be unlawful. Consistent with Wyeth v. Levine and Merck Sharp & Dohme v. Albrecht, the mere fact of EPA registration and an agency view that a warning is not required does not automatically establish impossibility preemption absent clear evidence EPA would have rejected the label change sought. Given FIFRA’s preservation of state authority over remedies and Bates’s emphasis on parallelism, I would not read § 136v(b) to create broad tort immunity where the claim plausibly mirrors FIFRA’s own adequacy-of-warning obligations.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FIFRA preempts a state-law failure-to-warn claim when EPA has affirmatively found the proposed warning is not required and federal law bars adding that warning to the pesticide label without EPA approval.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 7 U.S.C. §§ 136 et seq., especially the express preemption provision for labeling/packaging requirements (7 U.S.C. § 136v(b)) and the EPA registration/label-approval regime that makes unapproved label changes unlawful.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Monsanto argues that the respondent’s state-law failure-to-warn theory functions as a state-imposed labeling 'requirement' that is 'in addition to or different from' FIFRA’s federal labeling requirements, triggering express preemption under § 136v(b). Monsanto further contends that because EPA has determined the specific warning at issue is not required (and/or has rejected or effectively foreclosed it), Monsanto could not lawfully add the warning without prior EPA approval; thus, the state tort verdict creates a direct conflict by demanding a label change federal law prohibits absent agency permission. Monsanto and supporting amici emphasize the need for national uniformity in pesticide labeling and argue that allowing juries to impose divergent warning obligations undermines EPA’s expert risk-benefit judgments and the uniform federal label that FIFRA is designed to create.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Durnell argues that FIFRA does not categorically preempt state common-law failure-to-warn claims and that such claims can parallel (rather than add to) federal misbranding and labeling duties—i.e., state law can enforce the idea that a label must not be misleading or inadequate without creating a separate 'requirement.' Respondent is likely to contend that EPA registration/approval sets a federal floor and does not immunize manufacturers from state tort liability, and that Monsanto could have sought EPA approval to add stronger warnings (so compliance with both federal and state law was not impossible). Respondent also likely argues that an EPA judgment that a warning is not required does not necessarily carry the force of a binding prohibition sufficient to preempt traditional state remedies absent clear congressional command.
key_precedents: Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, 544 U.S. 431 (2005)
Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett, 570 U.S. 472 (2013)
Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht, 587 U.S. 299 (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Wyeth/Albrecht “clear evidence” argument remains the best response: an EPA conclusion that a warning is “not required” is not necessarily a federal prohibition, and tort law can sometimes run parallel to a federal misbranding floor. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, this case can and should be resolved on narrow express-preemption grounds under FIFRA § 136v(b) and Bates: given the record of EPA’s affirmative determination tied to the specific warning and the regime’s prior-approval constraint on label changes, the state verdict functions as a state-law “requirement for labeling” that is “in addition to” the EPA-approved label rather than an equivalent federal duty. Wyeth and Albrecht therefore do not control because they address implied conflict preemption in a different statutory setting and with a different unilateral-change mechanism; here, Congress expressly limited state labeling requirements, and the “parallel” characterization breaks down on these facts. I would keep the holding tightly cabined to circumstances where the agency has taken an authoritative position on the precise warning at issue, preserving room for other cases lacking that feature.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Wyeth/Albrecht require “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected the warning and that “not required” is not “forbidden”—does not overcome FIFRA’s express-text command that States may not impose labeling “requirements” “in addition to or different from” federal ones. Under Bates, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, a failure-to-warn verdict is itself a state “requirement for labeling,” and it survives only if it is genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard; once EPA has affirmatively determined the specific warning is not required within a regime that bars unilateral label changes, the state duty necessarily demands a different label than federal law presently allows. Albrecht, as Justice Kagan notes, is relevant only to whether agency action is sufficiently authoritative, and on this record the agency’s considered determination plus the prior-approval constraint establishes the requisite federal decision without importing Wyeth’s implied-preemption presumption. Even if a manufacturer could petition for an amendment, that possibility does not eliminate the present “in addition to” state requirement or the practical impossibility of complying with both regimes at once under Congress’s chosen uniform-labeling system.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best counterpoint: under Wyeth/Albrecht, EPA’s view that a warning is “not required” might not equal a federal prohibition, and absent “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected the precise warning, the state duty could be seen as merely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, this case is governed first by FIFRA’s express bar on any state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements; a jury verdict compelling a specific warning EPA has affirmatively deemed unnecessary operates as exactly that kind of additional labeling requirement under Bates, not a truly equivalent one. The practical consequence—highlighted by Justice Barrett—is that federal law generally withholds unilateral label-change authority, so the state command functions as an impossible mandate unless EPA grants permission, which is the kind of real-world conflict Congress sought to prevent through § 136v(b). Albrecht’s “clear evidence” framework does not displace that textual analysis here; at most it confirms that an authoritative agency determination about the warning’s necessity strengthens, rather than weakens, the express-preemption conclusion on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s point that FIFRA restricts unilateral label changes and that, if EPA has affirmatively said a particular warning is “not required,” a state verdict can look like an “additional” labeling requirement. But under Bates, the key question is whether the state duty is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard, and an agency decision not to require a warning at registration does not itself amount to a federal prohibition on that warning—nor does it satisfy Albrecht’s demand for an authoritative showing that EPA would have rejected the specific strengthened warning had the manufacturer sought an amendment. Mensing/Bartlett’s impossibility logic is weaker here because FIFRA contemplates registrant-initiated label amendments; absent “clear evidence” of rejection, the manufacturer’s compliance pathway is to ask EPA, not to claim categorical impossibility. Preserving traditional tort remedies in this posture respects Congress’s cooperative scheme and prevents EPA’s non-requirement determination from becoming, by inference, an immunity shield that disproportionately harms injured and vulnerable plaintiffs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson have the best point that, under Wyeth/Albrecht, an agency’s decision that a warning is “not required” is not automatically a federal prohibition, and absent “clear evidence” of rejection a state duty can sometimes operate in parallel. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, FIFRA’s express uniformity clause and Bates’s “equivalent-to-FIFRA” limit make this case turn less on implied conflict preemption and more on whether the tort verdict functionally imposes an additional labeling requirement when EPA has affirmatively addressed the specific warning and federal law bars unilateral label changes. On these facts, treating the state verdict as merely enforcing FIFRA’s misbranding floor collapses Bates’s distinction and would invite a de facto state-by-state relabeling regime that § 136v(b) was designed to prevent. Albrecht still matters for identifying when agency action is sufficiently authoritative, but here the record looks closer to an authoritative federal determination tied to the precise warning than to regulatory silence, so I remain with Petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point in urging Wyeth/Albrecht’s “clear evidence” framework and arguing EPA’s view that a warning is “not required” is not a federal prohibition. But that framing fits implied-preemption disputes under different statutes; here FIFRA’s text expressly preempts state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates permits tort suits only when they impose no more than FIFRA’s own misbranding standard. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, once EPA has affirmatively determined the specific cancer warning is not required and federal law generally forbids unilateral label changes, a state-law verdict demanding that warning necessarily operates as an additional labeling mandate rather than a parallel enforcement action. Under a separation-of-powers and textualist approach, we should not let state juries recreate a labeling regime Congress assigned to EPA and then insulated from divergent state requirements in § 136v(b).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that, under Wyeth/Albrecht, an agency decision that a warning is “not required” is not necessarily a federal prohibition, and without “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected the warning, state tort law might be viewed as merely parallel. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, FIFRA contains an express preemption clause aimed specifically at state “requirements for labeling,” and under Bates a failure-to-warn verdict becomes preempted when it effectively mandates label content “in addition to or different from” the EPA-approved label—particularly where federal law bars unilateral label changes absent prior EPA approval. On these facts, EPA’s affirmative determination regarding the specific warning, combined with the prior-approval constraint, makes the state verdict operate as an additional labeling requirement within § 136v(b) rather than a parallel misbranding claim. Albrecht’s implied-preemption “clear evidence” inquiry does not displace Congress’s textual choice for national uniformity in FIFRA, and the practical impossibility logic of Mensing/Bartlett supports that a State cannot use tort law to compel a label change the manufacturer lacks authority to make on its own.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best objection: under Wyeth and Albrecht, EPA’s statement that a warning is “not required” might not equal a federal prohibition, so absent “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected the warning, the state duty could be viewed as parallel to FIFRA misbranding. But that frame is mismatched to this case because FIFRA contains an express bar on state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates preserves only genuinely equivalent duties—not verdicts that functionally compel label language EPA has affirmatively deemed unnecessary within a regime that generally forbids unilateral label changes. As the Chief Justice notes, on this record the state verdict operates as an additional labeling mandate (not mere enforcement of a federal floor), and Justice Kagan’s point that authoritative agency action can be preemptive under Albrecht supports treating EPA’s considered rejection as the kind of federal determination that defeats the “parallel duty” characterization. Wyeth’s CBE pathway makes it materially different; here, the prior-approval constraint means the tort duty effectively demands what federal law withholds absent EPA permission.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrow express-preemption framing is the hardest for me because §136v(b) does target state “requirements for labeling,” and a tort verdict can operate as practical pressure to revise the label. But under Bates the key is whether the state duty is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s own misbranding baseline; EPA’s view that a particular warning is “not required” at registration does not, without a binding rejection of that warning’s substance, convert FIFRA’s floor into a federal ceiling. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Mensing/Bartlett-style impossibility also does not move me because FIFRA’s amendment mechanisms mean the manufacturer is not categorically forbidden from seeking the warning—so the necessary showing is Albrecht/Wyeth “clear evidence” that EPA would have disallowed it, which this record (as described) does not supply. On my pragmatic view, treating non-requirement as prohibition would broadly immunize inadequate-warning claims despite FIFRA’s own misbranding command, undermining procedural fairness for injured plaintiffs without a clear congressional directive.

John Roberts.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars States from imposing any labeling “requirements” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences, state common-law failure-to-warn duties are “requirements for labeling,” and they survive only if they are truly “equivalent to, and fully consistent with,” FIFRA’s misbranding provisions; where EPA has affirmatively determined the specific warning is not required and federal law makes unapproved label changes unlawful, a tort verdict demanding that warning functions as an additional state requirement rather than a parallel one. That combination also creates the sort of concrete impossibility/conflict identified in PLIVA v. Mensing and Mutual Pharmaceutical v. Bartlett because the manufacturer cannot unilaterally add the warning without EPA approval, so the state duty effectively compels what federal law withholds absent agency permission.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: FIFRA’s text expressly forbids States from imposing “any requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law failure-to-warn duties are “requirements for labeling,” and they are preempted when they do not run “parallel” to FIFRA’s labeling regime; here, EPA has affirmatively found the proposed warning is not required and federal law bars adding it without EPA approval, so the state verdict necessarily demands a label change beyond what federal law requires and permits. That creates both express preemption under § 136v(b) and a direct conflict (impossibility) because the manufacturer cannot unilaterally add the warning without prior federal permission, akin to the logic of PLIVA, Inc. v. Mensing and Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause provides that a State “shall not impose or continue in effect any requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” those required under FIFRA. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law failure-to-warn duties are “requirements for labeling,” and the only safe harbor is where the state duty is truly “equivalent to, and fully consistent with” FIFRA’s misbranding/labeling regime—something not satisfied where EPA has affirmatively determined the proposed warning is not required and federal law makes unapproved label changes unlawful. In that setting, the state verdict effectively compels a label change that cannot lawfully be made without EPA approval, creating the kind of direct conflict/impossibility recognized in PLIVA, Inc. v. Mensing and Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett, and it undermines Congress’s uniformity objective embodied in § 136v(b).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), bars only state labeling “requirements” that are “in addition to or different from” federal law, and under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC a state failure-to-warn claim survives if it enforces a parallel duty consistent with FIFRA’s misbranding prohibition against misleading or inadequate labels. An EPA determination that a particular warning is “not required” does not, without more, transform traditional state tort remedies into a forbidden additional requirement, especially where the manufacturer could have sought EPA approval for a stronger warning—making this case closer to Wyeth v. Levine’s presumption against preemption than to PLIVA v. Mensing’s impossibility regime. To find implied conflict preemption, Merck Sharp & Dohme v. Albrecht requires “clear evidence” the agency would not have approved the warning, and an administrative view that the warning is unnecessary (or even disfavored) is not necessarily a binding federal prohibition displacing state remedies. Preserving state-law accountability better aligns with FIFRA’s cooperative framework and avoids leaving injured individuals—often with limited power and resources—without meaningful recourse when federal oversight may not fully capture real-world harms.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under FIFRA’s express “Uniformity” clause, a state may not impose labeling "requirements" that are “in addition to or different from” those imposed under the Act. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Bates v. Dow Agrosciences recognizes that common-law failure-to-warn duties can qualify as “requirements for labeling,” and it permits them only when they are “equivalent to, and fully consistent with” FIFRA’s misbranding standards—not when they effectively demand a label change the federal regulator has affirmatively deemed unnecessary. Where EPA has specifically found the proposed warning not required and FIFRA makes it unlawful to alter labeling without prior EPA approval, the state tort verdict operates as a divergent labeling mandate and creates an unworkable conflict with the federal registration/label-approval scheme. See Bates, 544 U.S. at 446-47; cf. Merck Sharp & Dohme v. Albrecht, 587 U.S. 299 (2019) (treating agency action as potentially preemptive when it reflects an authoritative federal determination).

Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, state common-law duties can qualify as “requirements,” and they survive only if they are genuinely “equivalent” to FIFRA’s own misbranding standards—i.e., the manufacturer would be liable under state law only if it is also liable for misbranding under FIFRA. 544 U.S. 431, 443, 453–54 (2005). Where EPA has affirmatively determined the specific cancer warning is not required and federal law makes it unlawful to alter the label without EPA approval, a state tort verdict effectively compels a label change “in addition to” the federal scheme, creating at least express preemption under § 136v(b) and, in practical operation, an impossibility-type conflict akin to PLIVA, Inc. v. Mensing and Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett.

Dow Agrosciences LLC, 544 U.S. 431, 443, 446-47 (2005). Where EPA has affirmatively determined that the specific warning is not required and federal law makes it unlawful to add that warning to the label without prior EPA approval, a state-law failure-to-warn verdict effectively compels a label change that federal law does not permit—creating at minimum an impermissible additional labeling requirement and, in practical effect, a direct conflict. Respecting FIFRA’s nationally uniform labeling regime and EPA’s expert judgment, the state-law claim here cannot be treated as merely “parallel” to federal misbranding duties because it would force a warning EPA has found unwarranted.

Dow Agrosciences confirms that state common-law failure-to-warn duties are “requirements for labeling” subject to that clause. While Bates preserves only truly “equivalent” (parallel) state duties consistent with FIFRA’s misbranding standard, a verdict predicated on the absence of a specific warning that EPA has affirmatively found “not required” functionally imposes an additional state labeling requirement. Moreover, where federal law makes it unlawful to add unapproved label warnings and EPA’s considered action indicates the agency would not approve the warning, the state-law duty creates an irreconcilable conflict in the sense described by Mensing and Bartlett (and clarified in Albrecht), because the manufacturer cannot simultaneously comply with federal labeling constraints and the state-imposed command to warn.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), but under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC a state failure-to-warn claim survives when it “parallel[s]” federal misbranding duties rather than imposes a divergent label standard. EPA registration and an agency view that a particular warning is “not required” do not, without a clear and binding federal prohibition, categorically extinguish traditional state tort remedies; as in Wyeth v. Levine and Merck Sharp & Dohme v. Albrecht, the manufacturer must show “clear evidence” the agency would have disallowed the warning, not merely that the agency did not demand it. Because FIFRA’s regime contemplates manufacturer-initiated label amendments subject to EPA review, a jury verdict that enforces a non-misleading, adequate-warning duty can be treated as congruent with FIFRA’s misbranding baseline rather than an “additional” requirement, absent proof that EPA actually forbade the substance of the warning at issue.
